Georgia's government has unveiled plans for a hidden asset amnesty, enabling people to reveal undisclosed assets without facing prosecution.  
This initiative aligns with broader efforts to fight corruption and enhance transparency.  
Under the proposal, those who voluntarily disclose concealed assets will avoid criminal charges and instead pay a fee based on asset value.  
The government expects the amnesty to drive disclosures, boosting tax revenues and curbing corruption.  
Officials estimate billions are concealed abroad or unofficially.  
The move is part of a wider anti-corruption strategy endorsed by international bodies like Transparency International.  
Georgia has steadily improved in combating corruption and fostering business confidence, yet hidden wealth persists.  
Critics contend that offering amnesty undermines accountability.  
Supporters maintain it balances deterrence with cooperation.  
The government will run public awareness campaigns and set up a special unit within tax authorities to manage disclosures.  
The amnesty marks a key stride toward combating corruption and fostering transparency.

Viscount of Oxfuird is a Scottish peerage title established in 1651 for Sir John Maitland, 1st Baronet, a distinguished Scottish politician and lawyer.  
Sir John Maitland belonged to a notable Scottish family and held offices including Lord of Session, Lord of the Articles, and Lord Commissioner of the Treasury.  
He actively promoted the union of Scottish and English crowns and influenced negotiations resulting in the 1603 union.  
The 1st Viscount was succeeded by his son, John Maitland, 2nd Viscount, who joined the Scottish Privy Council and acted as Lord Lieutenant of Haddingtonshire.  
The 2nd Viscount's son, Charles Maitland, 3rd Viscount, was a leading military figure and served as general in the British Army during the War of the Spanish Succession.  
The 3rd Viscount's son, John Maitland, 4th Viscount, entered politics and represented Parliament for several years. He also supported arts and sciences closely.  
The 4th Viscount's son, James Maitland, 5th Viscount, was a key diplomat serving as ambassador to both Netherlands and France.  
He amassed significant collections of art and rare books, now preserved in the National Library of Scotland.  
The 5th Viscount's son, John Maitland, 6th Viscount, pursued politics and served in Parliament extensively.  
He also authored works on Scottish history and traditions.

Selective Publication in Nature Genetics: An Empirical Study of Abstracts  
Abstract: We investigate selective publication practices in Nature Genetics. We model the frequency of abstracts using logistic regression and assess whether journals differ in abstract frequency across authorship, issue, and field. Significant associations emerge, yet no differences are found between journal numbers (JSS).

Arie Lev Gruzman (born July 1, 1948) is an American academic specializing in Jewish studies. He currently directs the Center for Jewish Studies at Georgetown University.

Born in Tel Aviv, Israel, to Holocaust survivors, Gruzman earned his bachelor's degree from the Hebrew University of Jerusalem in 1969 and his Ph.D. in Near Eastern Languages and Civilizations from Harvard University in 1977.

Following his doctorate, Gruzman held academic appointments at the University of Pennsylvania and the University of California, Berkeley, before joining Georgetown's faculty in 1985. He has led the Center for Jewish Studies since 1995.

His research focuses on Jewish history, Jewish thought, and Judaism-Christianity relations. He has authored numerous works on these subjects, including "The Jews and the Dead Sea Scrolls" (1992) and "The Jewish Jesus: How Jewish Theology Influenced the New Testament" (2000).

Beyond academia, Gruzman has engaged actively in interfaith efforts. He has advised the Vatican's Pontifical Council for Interreligious Dialogue and served on the National Council of Churches' Committee on Faith and Order.

We propose a topological image segmentation method grounded in topological derivative for automatic sign language recognition. To segment hand gesture sequences from video, we employ watershed transformation to compute the topological derivative of gradient magnitude. Since gradient magnitude fails to meet topological derivative assumptions, we apply an isotropic filter to ensure suitable input.

The Fife Coalfield was a coal mining region in Scotland. It spanned primarily Fife, extending into neighbouring Angus and Kinross.  
The coalfield played a key role in Fife's economic development and provided employment for generations.  
The first mine opened in 1575, and the industry expanded significantly during the 18th and 19th centuries.  
At its height, it hosted over 300 mines and ranked among Britain's leading coal-producing areas.  
The coalfield declined early in the 20th century due to rising competition from alternative energy sources.  
The final mine shut down in 1966, marking the end of coal mining locally.

South Africa's government has revealed intentions to reopen its embassy in Mauritius, concluding a 20-year diplomatic rift.

Mauritius accused South Africa of backing separatist groups in the Indian Ocean nation during the 1980s and 1990s, prompting the closure of its embassy in Port Louis in 1997.  
Relations have notably improved recently, with both nations collaborating on anti-piracy efforts and regional stability.  
South Africa's foreign ministry stated that reopening the embassy would strengthen bilateral relations and enhance economic collaboration.  
"We see this as a crucial milestone in restoring ties," said spokesperson Clayson Mbatha.

Flemish Beef Roast (or Stew) with Vegetables  
Ingredients:  
- 1 2-3 lb beef roast, trimmed  
- 2 tbsp vegetable oil  
- 1 large onion, chopped  
- 2 carrots, chopped  
- 2 celery stalks, chopped  
- 3 cloves garlic, minced  
- 1 tsp dried thyme  
- 1 tsp dried rosemary  
- 2 tbsp tomato paste  
- 1 cup beef broth  
- 1 cup red wine  
- 2 cups chopped mushrooms  
- Salt and pepper, to taste  

Instructions:  
1. Preheat oven to 350°F.  
2. Heat oil in a large Dutch oven or pot over medium-high heat. Add roast and sear until browned on all sides, about 8 minutes per side. Remove roast and set aside.  
3. Add onion, carrots, celery, garlic, thyme, and rosemary. Cook briefly, stirring occasionally, until softened.  
4. Stir in tomato paste, broth, wine, and mushrooms. Bring to a gentle simmer.  
5. Season roast with salt and pepper. Return roast to pot, pouring vegetable mixture over top.  
6. Cover pot and place in oven. Roast for approximately 1 hour 15 minutes until beef is tender and veggies are cooked.  
7. Remove roast, let rest 10 minutes before slicing and serving. Serve vegetables separately.

Asparagus with Prosciutto di Parma, Pecorino Pepato, and Poached Eggs  

Ingredients:  
1 bunch asparagus (about 1 pound)  
6 large eggs  
4 tablespoons unsalted butter  
4 thin slices prosciutto di Parma, chopped  
1/2 cup grated Pecorino Pepato cheese  
1/2 cup heavy cream  
1/2 teaspoon white pepper  
1/4 teaspoon salt  

Instructions:  
1. Boil water in a pot over high heat. While doing so, fill a large bowl with ice water and set aside. Trim the tips off the asparagus and set aside. Cut stalks into 1-inch pieces and set aside. Blanch the tips in boiling water for 1 minute. Transfer to ice water using a slotted spoon and chill for 1 minute. Drain, pat dry, and set aside. Blanch stalks for 4 to 6 minutes until tender. Drain, pat dry, and set aside.  
2. Crack eggs into individual ramekins or cups. Heat a large skillet with water and add vinegar. Bring to a simmer over medium heat. Carefully lower eggs into water and cook 3 to 5 minutes until whites set and yolks are cooked to preference. Remove with a slotted spoon and drain on towel.  
3. Melt butter in a large skillet over medium heat. Add prosciutto and cook 2 to 3 minutes until crisp. Add asparagus and cook 2 to 3 minutes until tender-crisp. Stir in cheese and cook 1 minute until melted. Add cream, pepper, and salt; heat through.  
4. Serve by dividing asparagus and prosciutto onto individual plates. Place a poached egg atop each and add cheese sauce.

The novel centers on a fictional detective. He's known as Detective Caul, and the story begins with him and his friend. They find a body in the woods, discovered by an elderly man who calls police himself.  
After the death, the finder claims Caul might not be guilty. Police summon Caul to meet them at a tavern, but he declines. It's implied he has another case. Later, Caul arrives at the tavern and asks if the finder is still involved. Detectives agree to speak with him before arresting Caul. After gathering clues, Caul is shot in the head and the mystery resolves. However, the book never names who killed him—only suggesting suspects.  
Then it shifts to the next installment, where the killer is revealed, murdered similarly to Caul's friend. A trial follows, but Caul walks free. The narrator states: "It should have ended like that."  
This is why I consider this a genuine novel rather than a cheap fantasy.

Lavish Lemon Cake Recipe  

Ingredients:  
- 2 cups all-purpose flour  
- 1½ teaspoons baking powder  
- ¼ teaspoon salt  
- 3 large eggs, room temperature  
- 1 cup granulated sugar  
- 2 tablespoons lemon zest  
- ¾ cup fresh lemon juice  
- 1 cup buttermilk, room temperature  
- ½ cup unsalted butter, melted and cooled  
- 2 teaspoons vanilla extract  

Instructions:  

1. Preheat oven to 350°F (176°C) and grease a 9x13 inch baking pan with cooking spray or butter, then flour it.  

2. In a medium bowl, whisk together flour, baking powder, and salt. Set aside.  

3. In a large bowl, beat eggs and sugar until light and fluffy, about 3 minutes with an electric mixer. Fold in lemon zest and juice until blended.  

4. Gradually add dry ingredients to wet mix, alternating with buttermilk, starting and ending with dry components. Mix until just combined.  

5. Stir in cooled melted butter and vanilla extract until thoroughly mixed.  

6. Pour batter into prepared pan and smooth surface with spatula. Bake 25–30 minutes or until toothpick inserted comes out clean.  

7. Let cake cool completely before glazing. Combine powdered sugar and lemon juice in a small bowl until smooth. Drizzle over cake and let set before serving. Enjoy!

Tibor Grasser (born 1969) is an Austrian composer and pianist. He trained in piano at the Vienna Conservatory under Karl Leister and composition with Friedrich Cerha.

His compositions feature dissonance, intricate rhythms, and expressive dynamics. He has composed works for solo piano, chamber groups, orchestras, and opera. His music has been performed by renowned ensembles like the Vienna Philharmonic, Kölner Ensemble, and Ensemble Modern.

Beyond composition, Grasser is also a skilled pianist and has performed alongside artists such as Gidon Kremer and Yehudi Menuhin. He has released several albums featuring his own compositions, including "Piano Concerto No. 1" and "Symphony No.  1".

Ingredients:

- 3 cloves garlic, minced  
- 1/2 cup ricotta cheese  
- 1/4 cup grated parmesan cheese  
- 1/4 cup hot honey  
- 8 slices bread  
- 2 tablespoons olive oil  

Instructions:  
1. Preheat oven to 400°F.  
2. In a large bowl, combine broccoli florets, minced garlic, olive oil, and a pinch of salt and pepper.  
3. Spread mixture onto baking sheet and roast for 20–25 minutes until tender and lightly browned.  
4. While broccoli roasts, mix ricotta, parmesan, and seasoning.  
5. Remove broccoli from oven and lower temperature to 375°F.  
6. Toast bread slices until lightly golden.  
7. Remove bread and top each slice with ricotta mixture.  
8. Add roasted broccoli generously and drizzle with hot honey.  
9. Serve immediately and enjoy!

Coconut Fudge Brownies Recipe  

Ingredients:  
- 1 cup granulated sugar  
- ½ cup unsalted butter, softened  
- ¼ cup coconut oil, melted  
- 2 large eggs  
- 1 teaspoon vanilla extract  
- 1 ½ cups all-purpose flour  
- ¾ cup unsweetened cocoa powder  
- 2 teaspoons baking powder  
- ½ teaspoon salt  
- 1 cup semisweet chocolate chips  
- ½ cup shredded coconut  

Instructions:  
1. Preheat oven to 350°F (175°C) and line an 8x8 inch pan with parchment paper.  
2. In a large bowl, beat sugar, butter, and coconut oil until creamy. Add eggs one at a time, beating thoroughly afterward. Stir in vanilla.  
3. In a medium bowl, mix flour, cocoa powder, baking powder, and salt. Gradually incorporate into wet ingredients, stirring until combined.  
4. Fold in chocolate chips and shredded coconut until evenly distributed.  
5. Pour batter into prepared pan and smooth surface with spatula or spoon. Bake 25–30 minutes or until toothpick comes out clean.  
6. Cool completely before cutting and serving. Enjoy!
